title: Fear Whom?
hook: Does the Bible tell you to be terrified of God, or to stand in awe of Him?
tldr: The Hebrew "fear of the LORD" (YIR'AH) means awe and reverence, not terror. Luke 12:5 sits inside a speech telling disciples not to be afraid, and the Greek does not even name God. Read in context, it warns against hypocrisy and shame, and Matthew 10:28 speaks of destruction, not endless torment.
big_idea: Biblical fear of God is awe that draws you near, not terror.

points.title: YIR'AH means awe, not terror
points.text: The Hebrew word in "the fear of the LORD" describes the awe felt before something beyond us, like standing on a cliff edge or under a desert sky. Terror has different words: EIMAH and PACHAD.

points.title: The opposite of awe is the fool
points.text: Proverbs contrasts YIR'AH with a fool who despises instruction, not with fearlessness. Awe is the apprentice's respect for the master that makes learning possible.

points.title: God-fearers were drawn, not repelled
points.text: Paul addressed Gentile "God-fearers" who admired Israel's God and were attracted to Judaism. Their fear attracted them and fostered obedience and humility.

points.title: Translators added "God" to Luke 12:5
points.text: The Greek has only a neutral definite article (ton). The NASB capitalizes "Him" and the NLV inserts "God", while the KJV, ASV and NIV keep it neutral.

points.title: The context says: do not fear
points.text: Luke 12 repeatedly tells the disciples not to be afraid and stresses God's care for sparrows and numbered hairs. Instilling cosmic fear there would contradict the whole teaching.

points.title: Even if God, the warning is hypocrisy
points.text: The passage opens with the leaven of the Pharisees, hypocrisy. God can expose what is hidden, leading to shame like Gehenna; Matthew 10:28's "destroy" means cessation, not eternal torment.

sections.h: Two verses used to defend hellfire
sections.summary: Two unrelated verses are often cited by proponents of the Augustinian-Calvinist doctrine of hellfire: Proverbs 1:7, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge," and Luke 12:5, echoed in Matthew 10:28, "Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell."

sections.h: Old Testament fear: YIR'AH is awe
sections.summary: Standing atop the Eiffel Tower, at a boat's prow on the ocean, at a cliff edge or under a desert night sky brings awe and trembling: that is YIR'AH. Translations render it fear, awe, respect or reverence. Moses felt it asking to see God's glory (Exodus 33); Israel felt it when Moses came down Sinai with a shining face (Exodus 34). It means meeting something beyond one's abilities and comprehension.

Being scared of someone does not produce knowledge; you only study someone thoughtfully when you are in awe of them. YIR'AH acknowledges God's sovereignty and power. From the Hebrew root Y-R-A come YARE and YIR'AH, meaning reverence, respect or awe. Genesis 22:12 uses it of Abraham's respect and trust when he did not withhold his son.

In Proverbs 1:7 the contrast to YIR'AH is a fool who despises wisdom and instruction. If YIR'AH meant terror, its opposite would be fearlessness, not foolishness. Like an apprentice who respects a master craftsman and so learns the craft, awe of God makes learning possible; the fool is the apprentice who rejects the master's wisdom and never grows.

sections.h: Scared and terrified in the Bible
sections.summary: Hebrew has separate words for what we call fear: EIMAH (terror) and PACHAD (scare), used when someone fears for their life. Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10 use different words meaning awe or reverence. Wisdom begins with awe and respect for God, not with fearing He will kill you.

In the Antioch synagogue Paul addressed "Men of Israel and you who fear God" (Acts 13:16). "God-fearers" were Gentiles who revered Israel's God and were attracted to Judaism without fully converting (Acts 13:26). They were not terrified; they admired God's power, justice and goodness. Their fear attracted rather than repelled, motivating obedience, humility and a deeper relationship.

Luke 12:1-7: before a huge crowd, Jesus warns of the Pharisees' yeast, hypocrisy, says hidden things will be revealed, tells friends not to fear those who kill the body, says to fear him who can throw into Gehenna, then reassures them about sparrows and numbered hairs. Some hellfire advocates say Satan or we ourselves send people to hell, yet cite this verse to say we must fear God, a contradiction.

The NASB capitalizes "One," "Him" and "He," showing the translators' belief that the verse speaks of God. The NLV goes further and writes "Fear God." The KJV, ASV and NIV stay neutral with "him." The Greek ton is simply a definite article. The Greek meta, usually "after," can also mean "also" or "not only": fear the one who destroys not only body but also soul.

Luke 12 is about matters of the heart: being wise (12:1) and not fearful (12:4, 7). Jesus urges followers not to fear persecutors, reassures them of God's care (12:6-7), and repeats it in verses 22-32. He did not emotionally manipulate His young followers but taught with sincerity, kindness and respect. Ignoring context produced R.C. Sproul's contradiction: "On the one hand, we should fear Him. On the other hand, we should not fear."

sections.h: What if Jesus did speak of God?
sections.summary: Even granting the verse means God, Luke 12 opens with the leaven of hypocrisy: a righteous facade judging others while hiding evil, like "whitewashed tombs" (Matthew 23:27). In Judaism shame is as bad as death or worse (Bava Metzia 59a). Gehenna, a real place of burning waste and worms, symbolized deep shame. God can expose unrepented hypocrisy (Luke 12:2-3) and make one an outcast; sin corrupts the soul beyond physical death.

Nationally, this is exactly what happened. Israel's religious leaders did not turn from hypocrisy, leading to the devastation of Jerusalem and the temple and then exile. Many Jews faced poverty and homelessness, foraging for food, enduring what could be called a literal hell.

Matthew 10:28 echoes Luke 12 almost verbatim: fear him who can destroy (apollumi) both soul and body in Gehenna. Strong's Concordance defines apollumi as "to destroy, destroy utterly." Read literally as hellfire, it implies complete cessation of existence, body and soul, not the ongoing, unending suffering of Eternal Conscious Torment.

Some scholars say verse 5 means the reality of evil or social consequences of one's actions, fitting Luke's vigilance theme. Others say Satan: N.T. Wright argues Rome was the imagined enemy and the accuser, the satan, the real one, since the next verse presents God as trustworthy. Others say people in authority who can kill, shame your memory, or make you an outcast scavenging in the Valley of Hinnom. None fits Augustinian-Calvinist hellfire.

Fundamentalists also love Philippians 2:12, "work out your salvation with fear and trembling." J.B. Phillips, translator of The New Testament in Modern English, doubted Paul meant anxiety: fear destroys love, the Greek word can mean reverence or awe, and God has not given a spirit of fear (as Paul wrote to Timothy). The Corinthians received Titus "with fear and trembling" (2 Corinthians 7:15), so it is a conventional phrase for proper respect.

mythfact.myth: "The fear of the LORD" means being terrified that God will hurt you.
mythfact.fact: The word is YIR'AH: awe, reverence and respect. Hebrew uses EIMAH and PACHAD for terror. Its opposite in Proverbs 1:7 is the fool, not the fearless.

mythfact.myth: Luke 12:5 plainly names God as the one who throws people into hell.
mythfact.fact: The Greek uses a neutral article. Some translations capitalize or insert "God"; the KJV, ASV and NIV keep it neutral.

mythfact.myth: Matthew 10:28 proves souls suffer forever in hell.
mythfact.fact: Its verb apollumi means "destroy utterly." Read literally it implies cessation of body and soul, not endless conscious suffering.

mythfact.myth: "Fear and trembling" means living in nervous terror before God.
mythfact.fact: The Corinthians received Titus "with fear and trembling" (2 Corinthians 7:15); it is a conventional phrase for proper respect.

quiz.q: In Proverbs 1:7, what is set against the 'fear of the LORD'?
options: A fool who despises wisdom and instruction
quiz.why: If YIR'AH meant terror, its opposite would be fearlessness. Instead it is the fool, showing YIR'AH means awe that leads to learning.

quiz.q: What does the Greek of Luke 12:5 actually use for 'him'?
quiz.why: Ton is a neutral article. The NASB capitalization and the NLV's 'God' reflect translators' theology.

quiz.q: What does apollumi in Matthew 10:28 mean?
quiz.why: Strong's defines it as utter destruction, implying cessation of body and soul rather than endless conscious torment.

reflect: Does your picture of God make you want to draw near and learn, or to hide?
